Scheiner would rather see the nation adopt a single-payer system like the ones in Canada and Europe. The benefits, advocates say, is that pricey administrative costs are cut, resulting in large savings to patients. It's something that an up-and-coming coming state Sen. Obama talked about  six years ago. "I happen to be a proponent of a single-payer universal health care plan. ... But as all of you know, we may not get there immediately, because first we've got to take back the White House, and we've got take back the Senate, and we've got to take back the House," Obama said in 2003. But that position evolved during the campaign. "If I were designing a system from scratch, then I'd probably set up a single-payer system. But the problem is we're not starting from scratch," Obama said in Albuquerque, New Mexico, in August 2008. Now, the president favors giving Americans the option of joining a government-run plan that would compete with private insurers.  Watch more on the health care debate » . "Nobody is talking about some government takeover of health care. I'm tired of hearing that," Obama said in Raleigh, North Carolina, on Thursday. But Scheiner says that nobody has seen the details of that option, making it a hard sell for the president. "We don't even fully know what the public option is going to be. If the public option is too good, patients who are sick will flock to it, and I'm not sure it will be able to support itself." Scheiner almost had a chance to confront the president with his concerns. He was invited to a recent televised town hall meeting with Obama, but he says he was dropped from the program. "I just hope that the Congress, the American public and the president will hear some of my words," he said. "We've got to do something better." Scheiner finally had a chance to have his say Thursday. He and other doctors who support a single-payer system gathered in Washington to meet with lawmakers and rally supporters. ***

**WASHINGTON (CNN)** — While President Barack Obama frequently addresses the mounting opposition to his healthcare reform initiative, one prominent figure has remained relatively quiet—until now. 

Dr. David Scheiner, a Chicago-based physician who served as President Obama’s personal doctor for 22 years, has carefully evaluated the administration’s proposed reform and concluded that it is fundamentally flawed. "This isn't the kind of healthcare program that I think is going to work," Dr. Scheiner observed.

Dr. Scheiner’s critique carries unique weight. Beyond their 22-year professional relationship, he voted for the former Illinois senator in the 2008 presidential election. Today, however, he believes the President’s proposal falls short of true reform, arguing that its primary defect lies in maintaining a central role for private health insurance companies. 

"Everybody keeps saying we don't want the government involved in healthcare," Dr. Scheiner noted in an interview. "But the government is involved in Medicare, and it works."

Dr. Scheiner advocates instead for a single-payer model similar to those utilized in Canada and Europe. Under such a system, a single entity—typically a government agency—funds all medically necessary services, compensating doctors, hospitals, and healthcare professionals directly. Proponents emphasize that this approach dramatically cuts administrative overhead, resulting in substantial savings for consumers. 

This model aligns with views once expressed by the President early in his political career. "I happen to be a proponent of a single-payer universal healthcare plan," then-State Senator Obama stated in 2003. "...But as all of you know, we may not get there immediately, because first we've got to take back the White House, and we've got to take back the Senate, and we've got to take back the House."

By the time he ran for the presidency, his stance had evolved. "If I were designing a system from scratch, then I'd probably set up a single-payer system," candidate Obama explained in Albuquerque, New Mexico, in August 2008. "But the problem is we're not starting from scratch."

President Obama now advocates for a public option designed to compete directly alongside private insurers. Pushback against the plan prompted a firm response from the President during a speech in Raleigh, North Carolina, on Thursday: "Nobody is talking about some government takeover of healthcare. I'm tired of hearing that."

However, Dr. Scheiner contends that the ambiguity surrounding the public option makes it difficult for the administration to gain broad support. "We don't even fully know what the public option is going to be," he warned. "If the public option is too good, patients who are sick will flock to it, and I'm not sure it will be able to support itself."

Dr. Scheiner came close to raising these concerns directly with the President during a recent televised town hall, but he was ultimately removed from the broadcast's roster. "I just hope that Congress, the American public, and the President will hear some of my words," he remarked. "We've got to do something better."

On Thursday, Dr. Scheiner brought his message directly to the nation's capital. Joining a coalition of physicians advocating for a single-payer framework, he met with lawmakers and rallied supporters in Washington. Though he no longer serves as the President's personal physician, Dr. Scheiner remains dedicated to intervening—aiming, as he views it, to save the patient before it is too late.

*CNN's Ed Hornick and Brittany Cummings contributed to this report.*

The doctor’s comments come during a turbulent summer for the Obama administration's domestic policy agenda. Lawmakers returning to their districts for the August recess have been met with raucous town hall meetings, where conservative opponents have denounced proposed reforms as a "government takeover" of medicine.

President Obama has repeatedly argued that while a single-payer system might work well in other nations, transitioning the United States to such a model would be too disruptive to the millions of Americans who currently receive employer-sponsored health insurance. 

"If we were starting from scratch, then a single-payer system might make sense," Obama said at a town hall earlier this summer. "But we’re not starting from scratch. We have an existing system, and we need to build on what works and fix what doesn't."

"He’s a brilliant man, and I have tremendous respect for him," Scheiner said. "But on this issue, I think he’s letting the politicians and the lobbyists dictate the terms. We don't need a compromise that preserves the status quo. We need a system that puts patients before profits."

Instead, Scheiner advocates for a single-payer system, a nationalized insurance framework similar to Medicare for all, which would eliminate private health insurance companies from the equation entirely. 

The physician points out a stark contrast between President Obama’s current pragmatism and his stance as a rising political figure in Illinois. 

In 2003, while serving as an Illinois state senator, Obama explicitly endorsed a single-payer model during a speech to the AFL-CIO. "I happen to be a proponent of a single-payer universal healthcare program," Obama said at the time, adding that the country needed to "realize that we may not get there immediately."

Now, as president, Obama has repeatedly ruled out a single-payer system, calling it impractical for the U.S. given the existing market structure. He has instead argued that a hybrid model preserving employer-based coverage while offering a public option is the most realistic path forward.

For Scheiner, that shift represents a wasted opportunity and a surrender to special interests.

It is coming from his own political base — including the physician who cared for him for more than two decades.

Progressive activists and single-payer healthcare advocates are expressing growing frustration with the administration’s strategy, arguing that the White House has sidelined a government-run, single-payer system in favor of compromises designed to appease the private insurance industry.

Among the most prominent voices of discontent is Dr. David Scheiner, Obama’s personal physician in Chicago for 22 years.

"I am disappointed," Scheiner told CNN. "I think he's wasted a tremendous opportunity."

Scheiner, who treated Obama until he moved into the White House, has become an unlikely figurehead for the single-payer movement. He argues that the proposals currently floating through congressional committees leave the fundamentally flawed private insurance market intact.

As an Illinois state senator in 2003, Obama was explicit in his support for a single-payer model. Speaking to an AFL-CIO conference, he laid out a vision that aligns closely with what single-payer advocates are demanding today.

"I happen to be a proponent of a single-payer universal healthcare program," Obama said in 2003. "I see no reason why the United States of America, the wealthiest country in the history of the world, spending 14 percent of its Gross National Product on healthcare, cannot provide basic health insurance to everybody."

In that same speech, Obama acknowledged the political hurdles, adding: "A single-payer health care system, a universal health care system, may not get done immediately. We may not get there right away. But first we have to take back the White House, we have to take back the Senate, and we have to take back the House."

Now, with Democrats holding the presidency and commanding majorities in both chambers of Congress, single-payer supporters argue the time has come to deliver on that early vision.

However, President Obama’s stance shifted as he transitioned to the national political stage. By the time he launched his presidential campaign, he had adopted a pragmatic framework aimed at preserving employer-based coverage while filling in the gaps for the uninsured.

Addressing the issue at a town hall earlier this summer, Obama explained why he believes transitioning to a single-payer system is impractical for the U.S. at this time.

"If we were starting from scratch, then a single-payer system... might make sense," Obama said. "But we have a system in which the majority of Americans get their health care through their employers. And what I've said is, if you like your health care plan, you can keep it."

### The battle ahead

For single-payer advocates, that pragmatism feels like a missed historical moment. 

Liberal lawmakers in the House, led by Rep. Dennis Kucinich, D-Ohio, and Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vermont, continue to push for amendments that would allow individual states to implement single-payer systems, or at the very least, ensure a robust public option remains in the final bill.

Yet the White House remains focused on thread-the-needle politics, attempting to hold together a fragile coalition of moderate Democrats, key industry stakeholders, and reform-minded lawmakers.

For Dr. Scheiner, watching his former patient navigate the political minefield of Washington is a mixed experience. While he maintains personal affection for the president, his professional assessment of the pending legislation remains blunt.

"I love the man," Scheiner said. "I just think he's wrong on this one."

***

*CNN's Ed Henry and Dana Bash contributed to this report.*
